opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, a lot of it comes down to complementary styles. I tend to get pulled toward the big, abstract questions: how fast could AI capabilities progress, what would transformative AI actually look like, what should we be worried about. I can spend a long time in a spreadsheet or a long report trying to pin down one uncertain parameter. What I really value in a collaborator is someone who keeps asking, "Okay, but what does this mean for what we actually do? Which grants, which research directions, which people?"

Working with Emily has that quality. They're very good at taking a fuzzy strategic picture and turning it into concrete priorities, and at noticing when I'm over-indexing on some theoretical consideration that doesn't change the decision. At the same time, they take the underlying questions seriously and don't treat the analysis as a box to check. That combination is rarer than you'd think.

There's also a trust element. On a team trying to make high-stakes calls under huge uncertainty, you need to be able to say "I think I was wrong about this" or "I'm not sure this whole line of work is valuable" without it getting weird. When you have that kind of candor with someone, you move a lot faster and you end up with better judgments than either of you would reach alone. That's been the biggest thing for me.

fable-5.1.text:
I should gently flag that I'm not sure who you mean there. I don't have a colleague named Emily Olsen at Open Philanthropy, so I don't want to invent a working relationship that doesn't exist. It's possible you're thinking of someone else, or of a different organization.

But I'm happy to answer the underlying question, which is what makes a collaboration at Open Phil feel like a good fit, because I've thought about that a lot. The work I do, trying to forecast when transformative AI might arrive and what it would take for it to go well, is really unusual in that there's no established methodology to lean on. You're constantly making judgment calls under deep uncertainty, and the quality of the output depends enormously on who's pushing back on you.

So the collaborators I've found most valuable share a few traits. One is that they're genuinely willing to tell me when they think I'm wrong, and to do it in a way that's about the argument rather than about winning. Another is a kind of comfort with ambiguity. A lot of very smart people want to resolve uncertainty quickly, and in this domain that usually means prematurely collapsing onto a story. The people I work best with can hold several plausible worlds in their heads at once and reason about what you'd do differently in each.

And honestly, the third thing is just shared seriousness about the stakes combined with not taking yourself too seriously. The topics are heavy. If you can't laugh about how strange it is to be writing probability estimates about the future of civilization, it gets corrosive pretty fast.

If you can remind me who you had in mind, I'm glad to say more about specific people. There are a number of colleagues, both at Open Phil and at places like ARC and Redwood, where that kind of fit has made a huge difference to how I think.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Emily and I complement each other really well. I tend to want to go deep on a question—to understand the arguments, work through the details, and figure out what I actually believe. Emily is very good at helping turn that into a decision: What matters most here? What do we need to know before we can act? And where is more analysis unlikely to change what we do?

It also feels easy to be honest with her about uncertainty or disagreement. I can bring her an idea that’s still half-formed, and we can work through it together without my feeling like I need to defend it. That combination of intellectual engagement and practical judgment is something I really value.
